notes.claim: In a three-phase inverter six switches are driven by PWM signals, and the amplitude of each phase voltage is set by the duty cycle.
The motor's inductance filters the supplied PWM current into a three-phase sine wave with negligible harmonics.
Dead time turns both the high-side and low-side switches off before one turns on.
A double-conversion UPS rectifies the supply to power the inverter, and the loads run from the inverter output.
PWM is often used with an H-bridge, a configuration named for its likeness to the letter H.
Sine-triangle PWM works for three sine waves 120 degrees apart, as a three-phase inverter needs.
Dead time means one IGBT in a leg is always turned off first and the other turned on only after it, preventing a bridge shoot-through caused by unequal turn-on and turn-off times.
Dead time distorts the output voltage and current, so the smaller the dead time the better.
A double-conversion UPS has four main power elements: a rectifier, an inverter, a static bypass and a battery.
In double conversion the main power path is a rectifier and an inverter, so there is zero transfer time to battery.
In an online UPS the incoming AC is continuously rectified to DC and then turned back to AC by an inverter.
An online UPS drawing places the battery on the DC link between rectifier and inverter, with a bypass switch to the output.
IGBTs are mostly used in three-phase inverters, for variable-frequency drives that control the speed of AC motors and for UPSs.
A shore-to-ship converter statically converts 50 or 60 Hz port power to match a 60 or 50 Hz vessel network.
